title: Load weight
summary: What the load weight is, how 24 g and 28 g cartridges differ, what limit the rules of Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting set and how cartridges are checked.

body.html: The load is the weight of shot in a cartridge, in grams. The box shows it in large figures, for example '24 g' or '28 g'. In the USA and the UK it is sometimes given in ounces: 1 ounce is about 28 g.

The rules of Parcours de Chasse – Sporting™ and Compak® Sporting set the same limits. The load is at most 28 g of lead shot (up to 2% more is tolerated), so up to about 28.6 g, whatever the gauge. The shot must be round pellets of one size, 2.0 to 2.5 mm across (±0.1 mm). Reloaded cartridges, dispersers, mixed shot sizes, black powder and tracers are forbidden.

html.sporting: Before you start at a stand, the referee may ask for two of your cartridges to check: one from the right vest pocket and one from the left.
html.compak: If a check shows that your cartridges break the rules, all the shots you fired with them before that check count as zero, that is, as a miss. The jury may let the results stand if you could not have known and gained no advantage, provided the fault is put right as soon as it is found.

body.html: Many Sporting™ shooters use 28 g in competition: more pellets give a denser pattern, especially on far targets. The downside is heavier recoil, and over a day of 100–200 targets you feel it.

24 g cartridges are lighter, push less and are usually a little cheaper. For practice and for close and medium targets they are usually enough and less tiring; on far targets 28 g gives a denser pattern. Even lighter 21 g loads exist, mostly for 20 gauge or for teaching.

Many coaches suggest that beginners start with 24 g. Less recoil means less fatigue and less risk of learning to flinch before the shot. You can move up to 28 g later, once your technique is consistent.

key_points.html: The load is the weight of shot in grams; 1 ounce is about 28 g.
Limits: 28 g lead (+2%), pellets 2.0–2.5 mm; no reloads, mixed shot, black powder or tracers.
28 g gives a denser pattern on far targets; 24 g is softer for practice and beginners.
Sporting™: the referee may check two cartridges; Compak® Sporting: shots with non-compliant cartridges count as zero.

did_you_know.html: 1 ounce is 28.35 g, so the classic British '1 oz' cartridge almost exactly matches the FITASC 28 g limit.

quiz.q: What is the maximum shot load under FITASC rules?

options.text: No limit, any load is allowed

quiz.explain: Both disciplines allow at most 28 g of lead shot, +2%.

quiz.q: Why do many coaches suggest 24 g cartridges for beginners?

options.text: They push less and are less tiring
Only they are allowed for beginners
They fly further than heavier loads

quiz.explain: Less recoil helps keep good technique and avoid a flinch.

quiz.q: How many cartridges may the referee take for checking in Sporting™?

options.text: Two, one from each vest pocket
The whole box from the bag

quiz.explain: The referee may take two cartridges, one from each vest pocket.
